title: Sub-Gaussian Confidence Intervals for Heavy-Tailed Data: Characterizing the Limits of Inference
claim: Competing intervals lose coverage as tails get heavier; ours stays valid at the cost of somewhat longer intervals.
layout: 6 line plots in 3 rows by 2 columns, length left and miscoverage right
description: A grid of six line plots with three rows and two columns. Each row is a distribution setting with tail parameter alpha = 1, 0.25 and 0.1. The left column plots mean interval length against the miscoverage level delta. The right column plots empirical miscoverage against delta, with a dashed y = delta target line. Each plot has three curves: DLLO in blue with circles, our approach in red with crosses, and Student-t in green with triangles. Legends sit below each plot, and the panels are captioned (a) to (f). In the top row, our approach sits between the other two methods. In the lower rows, our curve is the longest, but its miscoverage stays near zero or below the target. DLLO and Student-t climb well above the dashed line, and DLLO reaches about 0.6 at alpha = 0.1.
caption: Comparison of mean interval length and empirical miscoverage for DLLO, our proposed adaptive approach, and the Student-$t$ interval under the considered mixture distributions. The dashed line in the right panels is the target miscoverage level $y=\delta$.
abstract: We investigate the problem of uncertainty quantification in the mean estimation framework. Given an i.i.d. sample from a distribution with unknown mean $Î¼$ and variance $Ï^2$, we want to construct an estimator $\whÎ¼_n$ and provide a computable and size-optimal upper bound for the error $|\wh Î¼_n - Î¼|$. While estimators possessing strong deviation guarantees are well known, no data-dependent non-asymptotic upper bounds for their performance exist in general. We show that this gap can be bridged by introducing a parameter that characterizes the ``effective sample size'' available for uncertainty quantification. This parameter captures the difficulty of the problem, interpolating between ``easy'' cases where sub-Gaussian confidence intervals exist and ``hard" cases where their construction is impossible. Using this characterization, we design confidence intervals of optimal length that are fully adaptive to the unknown variance. Numerical experiments confirm that our approach maintains nominal coverage even in asymmetric and heavy-tailed regimes where other existing methods fail.
